subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, listening a while ago to the parliamentary secretary while glancing through the bill, I was convinced that it exclusively concerned government employees and officials in the Northwest Territories. I thought that if the bill merely concerned public servants and officials in the Northwest Territories, it had a very limited scope. The bill merely provides that the employees cannot become shareholders of a company dealing for example with read estate and mines to purchase such real estate.
For my part, Mr. Speaker, I was thinking about Quebec. I will say a word in a while about the comments of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). If the bill is not altered as far as public servants are concerned-and when I refer to civil servants I do not include owners and residents-I think that it should also prevent them from belonging to a company trading in the Northwest Territories.
Hon. members probably heard of the current investigation in northern Quebec, the investigation by the Quebec government. I suggest this will not get very far, because it is a question of defrauders investigating other defrauders in the same party. All this is caused by conflicts of interest at the public service level. Some public servants get rich at the expense of the provincial or federal governments. And everything is so well schemed that they have their spokesmen here in Ottawa, in Quebec, in our area. There is no way this could be undone. Everything is schemed, as the saying goes. Money goes into pockets all year long. People believe moneys voted go to Indians, Eskimos, Inuits. But the main part is pocketed by public servants.

subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext: What!

subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext:
Somebody said: What! Why should he show surprise? He knows full well.
This is why I say that the first part of the bill does not go far enough. It should include provisions for public servants who hold equity shares in marketing companies, snowscooter companies, arms companies. They triple their salaries with what they get from their involvement with those companies.
The bill is restricted to Yukon public servants. The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), who spoke this afternoon, advised us of a good many things. I did not know people in Yukon could not own their own tract of land. This is fantastic. It is just as amazing as what happened in our area during land reform, where a third of farmlands were eliminated by people who did not even know what farmland is, people who said those lands were not good farmland. Second generation farms were said to be uncultivable.
I feel the problem in Yukon is much more serious than commonly believed and this is why I say the hon. member for Yukon is right when he talks about Yukon owners, people living in the Yukon, because, here, I would like to make a distinction among public servants: In the Yukon, some public servants come from the area and some do not. It is obvious that those who do not should not be entitled

to buy shares in these companies or to take part in transactions. But it is another matter when we are talking about a Yukon resident, Mr. Speaker. I believe that those who live in the Yukon should be entitled to ownership just like people in other parts of Canada.
I am not saying that they should take control of the mines, for instance, and be the main shareholders, but I believe that they should have certain rights. And I believe that the act is too restrictive because it considers on an equal basis all the civil servants who live in the Yukon, those who live here in Ottawa, and then went to the Yukon or to another province in the name of the government to earn their living. Mr. Speaker, I am simply saying that this bill will be referred to the standing committee of this House, but that it is essential to amend it. It is not at all advantageous for the Yukon and does not protect the public servants, wherever they may be.

subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is already obvious from the discussion that is taking place here today that there are a lot of anomalies in land use north of the sixtieth parallel.
Remarkably enough, even though the theme of developing Canada's last frontier, and the theme of northern development seem to be espoused by all Canadians today, the government still has the viewpoint that with respect to land use it must keep a strong, monopolistic control over the policy to the ridiculous extent that was outlined by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) with respect to total prohibition of agricultural development in both the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
I remember that when I was the minister of the department, to make things a little more human and humane in interdepartmental communications, of which the flow never ceased, we used to have a caption at the top of the memorandum that went something like this, "Woe unto them who sit on their frozen assets." This seems to be the policy that is being re-endorsed by the bill before us this afternoon. It does not do anything to resolve the restricted land use problems. It certainly does not do anything to deal with the bureaucratic bungling that has been typical of land use pronouncements since Canada finally became interested in the development of its great northern heritage.
When the Department of Northern Affairs was first set up, the late Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent said that Canada had been exercising for far too long its responsibilities for development of its northern frontier in a state of absentmindedness. I am sure that is the only description that can be used in reviewing Bill S-20 that is before us this afternoon.
I wish to expand on some of the points made by the hon. member for Yukon with respect to the unbelievably bureaucratic approach to agricultural development in northern Canada. There is absolutely no policy on farming north of the sixtieth parallel. What has happened as a result of the decree that came from Caesar Augustus on January 10 last to the effect that there was to be a total suspension of the disposition of federal Crown land for agricultural use in both the Yukon and Northwest Territo-
April 11, 1975

ries? I think it has brought the foolishness of the situation into clear perspective.

subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext: And the cancellation of existing land leases.

subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext: Yes. I will deal with that in a moment. The decree that came from the minister on January 10 was for prohibition of any further alienation. It also included the cancellation of existing leaseholds. The problem has been brought into focus by the Northwest Territories Farmers' Association. It is true that there is sufficient interest in farming in the Northwest Territories to have an association.

subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext: And in the Yukon.

subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member for Yukon that this is developing on parallel lines in both the territories. As a result of the negative policy that was forthcoming, the Northwest Territories Farmers' Association gathered together to discuss the dilemma. They were particularly concerned about the Benoit family who had moved into the area near Fort Providence and were operating at the Horn River in the Northwest Territories. They had invested in their farm four years of their time and all their savings. The project had received encouragement from the government of the Northwest Territories. Indeed, it was the government of the Northwest Territories that encouraged the Benoits and other enterprising Canadian citizens like them to venture into the northern part of Canada and pioneer in establishing a viable agricultural industry.
It was a tip-off from a member of the territorial government that first brought this problem to my attention. I have been able to research the matter further in some of the colourful newspapers that are published in the Northwest Territories. I shall be dealing later with some of the interesting comments in the newspaper published at Fort Smith under the name The Pilot.
I should like to refer to another strange anomaly to be found within the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Under the decree to which I have referred, the department ordered the Benoits off the land within 90 days-this, Madam Speaker, notwithstanding the fact that they had invested considerable sums of money, that they had had the encouragement and support of the territorial government of the Northwest Territories, and that in attempting to assist this family in their worthwhile efforts to establish a herd of cattle, the government of the Northwest Territories had been supplying them with feed. Yet in the face of these concrete realities we have a decree suspending this activity, that forces them off the land, and which says they have to wait two or three years until an agricultural policy can be formulated.

subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext: They were told to get off.

subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext: Yes, I said they were ordered off the land. No decision apparently can be made for a period of two or three years. This must be bureaucratic bungling gone mad.

subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext:
It is not bungling; it is intentional policy.
Territorial Lands Act

subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext: Well, whatever it is, I trust that the parliamentary secretary will convey the message to his minister, who I am sorry is not here today to hear some of these comments. He is the kind of man who, if he were aware of the implications in terms of human privation, would not have anything to do with policy enunciations of this kind. I wonder whether there was any consultation with the Department of Agriculture. When you are dealing with agricultural policy in a part of Canada one would think the Department of Agriculture would be consulted.

subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext: That would make things worse.

subsubtopic: CORPORATIONS IN WHICH GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES PROHIBITED FROM ACQUIRING INTEREST
speechtext:
I do not think it could be any worse, and I hope it would be better. I also wonder what has happened to the excellent experiment that had been going on for a period of 20 years at Fort Simpson. I read with some degree of concern that this experimental station, which I had the opportunity to view when I was minister, had been phased out, and at the time it seemed to me that this was a retrograde step. However, I was not at all aware that the situation had deteriorated to the level indicated by the problem that was outlined here today.
Let me deal with the matter in terms of the colourful writing that comes out of the Northwest Territories and Yukon by the people who are actually grappling with the real problems of human and resource development north of 60. In its issue for February 20, 1975, The Pilot carries this headline: "There's an awful smell of bull manure and it's not from the farmers' feet." The article goes on to report the meeting of the Northwest Territories Farmers' Association which tried to get some justice and to find a sensible solution to the problems facing the farmers in the Northwest Territories. More to the point, Madam Speaker, in the editorial column the subject is dealt with under the heading "Is democracy dead in NWT?" The editorial stated:
The plight of the farmer in the Northwest Territories, as reported on page 1, only goes on to prove even more conclusively the need for immediate provincial status for the north.
The fact that one department of government can control everything in the north from development of land to the development of nonrenewable resources, almost without reference to other government departments, and most certainly without reference to the people who are most directly involved-us-is nothing less than a complete and utter waiving of our rights as Canadian citizens.
If I may interpolate, how many times have we heard that complaint as we have travelled, for example, into the north as representatives of the Indian affairs committee? Then further along in the editorial:
Again it is a case of the civil servant sitting behind his Ottawa desk, who has probably never been further north than his television set, dictating what we can and cannot do north of the 60th parallel.
The whole of Canada was built by people with a little imagination, a little money and a hellofa lot of hard work-a term which most of the Ottawa oafs think means bending paper clips into grotesque shapes. The west would still be buffalo range if there were not a few adventurous souls willing to "take a chance" on making a living outside the boundaries of civilization at that time. Today, the north is no different. It is still going to take people with a little imagination-
They mean people like the Benoits, who are being persecuted because of their initiative.
-a little money and a hellofa lot of hard work to make a viable living in the north if they want to retain any semblance of independence.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
At the recent "Focus North Conference" in Edmonton, the delegates sent a strongly worded telegram to Judd Buchanan, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in support of territorial farmers.
Perhaps Mr. Buchanan would like to live up here and pay $1.17 for a dozen eggs, or $2 for a loaf of bread as is common in many northern communities. If he had to survive in the north as an independent businessman he would soon find out that there is precious little heat or food in the bureaucratic bullshit that his department continuously serves the north.
I trust that having referred this bill to the committee on Indian affairs we might be able to bring in some amendments and also get some answers regarding the negative attitude toward agricultural policy, so as at long last to make it possible for any Canadian to live in the parts of Canada north of 60 with the same opportunities, rights and privileges as Canadians who live in other parts of Canada.

speechtext: that Bill C-30, to repeal the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REPEAL ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, ordinarily the business of repealing an act that has been on the statute books of Canada for nearly 40 years would be a regular matter of housecleaning or housekeeping, but this particular act has some things which I think will cause us to ask that this bill be delayed. Let me make my reasons clear.
In all fairness I think I should say that this act was placed on the statute books as a result of the efforts of the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner before the war, and many people look on it as his monument. When a man has moved on he likes to look back at something he has done as his own. I should think that the Right Hon. Mr. Gardiner, who sat for 20 years on the government side of this House and one year in the opposition, had the right to consider the

PFAA as a very worthwhile piece of legislation. We are now meeting here some years later to dismantle this monument to that long time minister of agriculture.
The act itself seems irrelevant today because the maximum payment under the act was $800. The act was the result of 10 years of depression and drought on the prairies, and its purpose was to give farm families enough money in case of a crop failure to pay their taxes, to buy their groceries for the winter, and have enough to seed their crop the following year. It should be said loudly and clearly that this act was a lifesaver for the many families that survived the 10 worst years in the history of agriculture in western Canada.
In addition the act gave those of us who were interested in policy precise crop figures for every quarter section in the west, and on the basis of that information we were able to do many things. We were able eventually to set up crop insurance legislation and to decide which areas would be good for community pastures and which would be good for other purposes. It was one of the first steps in a sort of land use policy which has slowly taken hold among governments in the western world. The PFAA should be given the credit it deserves.
It is true that the machinery of the act was awkward in the beginning and it was necessary to reform it. To get crop insurance in the event of a crop failure you had to be farming within a block of land where the crop yield was below a certain number of bushels. These blocks were too large in many cases and there could be several families with terrible crops, no income, and facing a difficult winter because the average for their block was higher than the minimum allowed under the act.
In this reform to the legislation we made these blocks smaller and we changed their size to allow for different types of land with different types of crops because of different weather, and I think that in the last years of its operation it was working reasonably well.
There are other things I wish to say about this act. It required inspectors to visit each farm where the crops had failed. Unfortunately for the history of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, some of the inspectors, if not all of them, began to relate their duties in inspecting crops and the yield to the political persuasions of the farmers involved. This became what the political scientists describe today as "the Gardiner machine". This political machine set up on the prairies matched in efficiency, interest, and detail Tammany Hall of New York City, which is over 100 years old.
It fell to the lot of the Diefenbaker administration to clean up this legislation, and this was done without the dismissal of a single inspector, supervisor or senior employee under that legislation. All we did was ask them as fieldmen to refrain from political activity at the time of an election. In fact we went further and instructed the supervisors to hire the best men in each district, regardless of political persuasion, and we set an example, which I think will be admitted freely by the farmers in the west was good, by trying to pick reeves or councillors, men who had been elected in local areas and who were highly regarded for their integrity and ability. As a result, the farmer whose farm was being inspected would know he had a fair inspector and did not have to pass the test of
April 11, 1975

belonging to or working for the Liberal party. So the PFAA, administered fairly, became a very useful act.
I mention these things because no party suffered greater complaints than did we at the time. It was only natural and human that after 22 years with one administration all the available jobs went to supporters of that one party, and the people felt that when a different party formed the government it should take over this operation. We were criticized by members of our own party for following this practice of not dismissing those who had been appointed by the previous administration, and for going out of our way to see that the very best men of all parties were selected to be field inspectors.
One of the men who was appointed to head up the PFAA as a director was Mr. Howard Riddell, known over the province for his honesty and integrity as municipal secretary. His instructions by the minister involved only one thing, and that was to run the PFAA honestly and well.
I remember a quarrel that developed in this House in 1962 over the appointment of an individual to investigate charges that certain farmers were abusing the PFAA. The matter was sent to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. At that time I was the minister. I appeared before that committee, threw away all my rights as a minister, and said that my records and communications between myself and the PFAA were available for the examination of the committee. There was no hiding of documents.
What I am saying is contained in the records of that standing committee. When members of parliament from all parties on the committee heard the evidence and saw the record, they immediately dismissed the charges. One member was not satisfied. I hear an objection. This was in the period of 1964 when the charges finally came up in the House. There was no Liberal majority of members on that committee. It was a minority parliament. Members from all parties agreed that the PFAA had been run well. There was one exception. One member said that politicians were scratching each other's backs and suggested that the charges should be brought before a court. They were. Once again, this time as the ex-minister, I threw all my records and personal communications into the hands of the courts. All the officials gave evidence.
The judge in his ruling threw out the charges on the basis that there was no evidence of malfeasance and that, on the contrary, all the evidence was clear that the instructions always had been that this act was to be administered honestly and fairly. That particular member of parliament sat on this side of the House. I refer to the member who made the request that the matter be taken before a judge. He received his pay-off by being called to the cabinet on the other side of the House where he became Minister of Agriculture. When the people caught up with him in 1972 he went back to the farm where he is today. I give this history because this particular bill to repeal this legislation is a matter of some interest to many farmers.
We now face a situation in the west where the political machine that we hoped we had destroyed in the years between 1957 and 1963 is being built up again. This time,
Prairie Farm Assistance Act
however, there are new ministers. This situation started when the government decided to believe, in 1969 and 1970, that the information it was receiving from the experts, Statistics Canada and Statistics Washington, showing that there was too much grain. The government decided to take the farmers out of production. It said to them that if they did not go out of production they would lose their right to sell wheat, but that if they did as they were told and summerfallowed they would be paid $6 an acre, or if their land was put into grass they would be given so much per acre.
One can see the possibilities for corruption creeping up again. The power of this parliament was being used to take away the right of a man to sell his grain unless he did what he was told. If he did what he was told then he might be paid these sums of money. Once you start a system of telling farmers what they have to do, you must have a force of field inspectors to see how much land is in grass and how much is in summerfallow. Planes flew over the prairies photographing every square inch with cameras which could even see a golf ball.
After time had passed and all the money had been paid out for the grass program and the summerfallow program, it was discovered that there were overpayments. The government announced that it would take back the money. So, once again an army of inspectors had to be organized to go out and collect the overpayments that were made to the farmers. To add to the confusion of having all these inspectors going out, elections were being fought and funny instructions were given to inspectors. They were told that if an argument developed they were to juggle the figures for the benefit of the farmer. This type of thing does not pass unnoticed in western Canada.
On December 9 last year I asked a question of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I asked it with the knowledge of the quick action the government took in responding to a request for an inquiry in the province of Quebec when trouble developed there. I asked:
Would the minister take personal note of the disturbing events in the administration of Prairie Farm Assistance Act in the west? I am referring specifically to unauthorized payments for field men during the election period, information about which the hon. member for Red Deer has in his possession. In view of these disturbing developments, would the minister consider asking Mr. Howard Riddell, who was for 14 years the head of PFAA and who is now working for the Department of Municipal Affairs in Saskatchewan and who has the confidence of the farmers, and who is well known for his honesty and integrity, to come back and check out this very smelly situation?
I made no charges and named no names. I simply asked the Minister of Agriculture last December to check out this smelly situation. The minister replied:
I do not know what the situation is, but I will certainly check on it and ascertain what the facts are.
Then I went on and suggested that he might consider asking Mr. Williams, the then Deputy Minister of Agriculture in Ottawa, to do the checking. I suggested that he let someone who is impartial, and known for his honesty and integrity, check on these facts. Later on in the week the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) asked the minister about the possibility of asking the RCMP fraud squad to take this matter under investigation.

Madam Speaker, I thought perhaps the mover of the motion would introduce it with a few words, but since he has not done so I should like to address myself to the matter for a few minutes.
I commend the admirable sentiments of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) in presenting this motion. In calling for a national youth appreciation week the hon. member is expressing his respect and concern for this country's youth which, I am sure, all hon. members share. I am glad that he has chosen to change his bill to a motion because otherwise I would perhaps have had to question the usefulness of such proposed legislation. When a subject becomes law, it is a serious matter that goes onto the statutes of our country, and this would open the door to all kinds of groups wishing to have a law passed in order to back their favourite cause, whether it be a week for senior citizens, a week for young farmers, or a week for another group in our society.
It is of course impossible to argue against the sentiments that underlie this motion. However, I would like to see a little more detail, something more concrete, and a better explanation of what lies behind the motion. What effect would this motion have on the different segments of our youth? For example, what specifically will a child of 12 or a senior high school student derive from this motion? I believe that there is always the danger of negativism.
Not very long ago students on a great many campuses, in this country and elsewhere, were exceedingly vocal in their criticism of the establishment's so-called mindless rhetoric. The criticisms may be less vocal now but I believe they persist, and with some reason. I would not like to see this kind of idea, which we all support, being placed in the category of what is sometimes called mindless rhetoric. It has become platitudinous to associate youth with cynicism, but platitudes are often platitudes simply because they are true.
Surely we must take care not to excite youthful cynicism by needlessly indulging in empty rhetoric. I am afraid there is always this danger when we provoke motherhood type resolutions in the House. Therefore, I would like to see something more specific suggested in this respect. The sentiment, of course, as I said before, is shared by all members of the House, and is certainly shared by the government. Indeed, it is the underlying motivation of several of the government's programs that are oriented toward the youth of Canada. So perhaps, rather than a week being dedicated to our youth, in practice perhaps all the year round is so dedicated so far as many of us are concerned.
This year the government's Summer '75 program involves 12 government departments, with an expenditure of over $67 million. The summer program is expected to provide direct and indirect employment and activities for almost half a million students. This certainly shows the feelings that the government has in trying to encourage our young people and to show our appreciation of them.
The Department of the Solicitor General will employ a number of students in connection with its participation at the 5th U.N. Congress on the Prevention of Crime and Treatment of Offenders. This will take place in Canada later this year. Other federal departments are involved in
April 11, 1975

providing student employment and activities for the coming year.
We are all familiar, of course, with the OFY program which started a few years ago and went through many birth pangs. Many people criticized it when it first began, myself included, but it is something that has had many of the wrinkles ironed out of it, and it has given an opportunity to many young people to develop their own kinds of projects. It has allowed them to express themselves. I think this in itself is a great show of appreciation on the part of the government for our young people. Of course, Opportunities for the Youth is again the major component of the government's summer program this year. The OFY program has an estimated budget of $27.5 million, and it should provide some employment and useful activity for about 20,000 of our young people.
The Department of the Secretary of State is also sponsoring other summer programs this year. The student community services program is designed to support and encourage the activities of voluntary organizations serving the community by enabling these organizations to employ young people. That program has a budget of $5.7 million and will employ over 2,000 students. It will also involve several thousand volunteers. The department is also responsible for organizing a youth hostel program and a travel and exchange program. This travel and exchange program, in my view, is something that should be expanded much more. I feel that it is one of the greatest boons to Canadian unity. It permits the young people to travel about in our country, to get to know and understand people from other parts of Canada, and certainly understanding is what is needed to foster national unity.
LIP, although it is not directed primarily at young people, is a significant improvement over traditional winter works programs, and it is the kind of innovative community-oriented concept that would have been a welcome suggestion had it come from any party. I take pride in the fact that it has come from the government side of the House. Of course it has received much support from all sides of the House.
Apart from these important programs for summer employment I believe there exists a need and an opportunity for greater direct involvement of federal departments and agencies in the lives of young people, especially in the areas of education and the arts.
In light of the rather depressing results of recent surveys undertaken by the Committee for an Independent Canada with regard to students' awareness of their country, I believe that the government should give consideration to expanding the programs of the various cultural agencies as they affect young people. The very successful museumobile is a concept which deserves to be explored and expanded more fully.
The principles of democracy and decentralization which are the professed aims of government policy in the areas of museums, the performing arts and visual arts, are yet to be adequately acted upon, Madam Speaker. The need for greater activity in this area is acute, especially as it affects the lives of our children. We have a responsibility to promote participation among our youth in the affairs and
Youth Appreciation Week
activities of the community which surrounds and often dwarfs them. Their considerable energy and imagination needs to be harnessed, for their sake and for ours, and put to good use. We need, further, to encourage that element of our youth that at present is not organized in the way youth groups are. There is a crying need to respond in very concrete and realistic ways to that wasted youthful energy which devotes itself to outward destructive, and ultimately self-destructive, pursuits. The euphemism we often use is delinquent, but they are our children, and they are troubled. We have an important responsibility to them.
There exists in the east end of Montreal a huge project taking shape, a grand sporting complex intended to accommodate the Olympics. It is ironic that it should be located in that particular part of Montreal where children play in the streets. It would be a travesty if those magnificent facilities were to lay dormant after the Olympic flame is extinguished, and that is the fear of many people in this country. They say that in Munich the facilities which were made available for the Olympics there have not been used nearly to capacity, and I hope that this will not be the case in Canada.
I do not know if this is the proper time to mention it, but since we are talking about appreciation of our youth, and since we are talking about sports and other things which are good for our youth-because we know the old saying, which is perhaps a cliche, that a healthy mind exists only in a healthy body-we should be concerned about the future use of the Olympic area in Montreal, and I would suggest that perhaps it could become an ongoing national sporting centre for our young people from all over Canada and kept in good use for the benefit of our young people.
In closing I simply want to repeat that I admire the sentiments being brought forth in this motion. I simply wanted to put a few words on the record in order to show my support for that kind of sentiment, and also to underline the fact that we must be more specific when we suggest this kind of thing, whether it be for young people or for other elements of our society.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I had not intended to say very much because I think I spoke about this motion in the last parliament. I have certainly done much work on it. I think most hon. members have received letters from Optimist International, and I want to make sure that all hon. members realize that great job Optimist International did for the members of this House when we played the members of the press gallery at our annual hockey game. They are the ones who sponsored it and treated us very well and did an excellent job, and we would like to thank them for that assistance.

Of course the members of parliament beat the press gallery, and I think we are all in better shape.
I would like to read one thing into the record. The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) has organized national youth appreciation week every year, and he puts out a very nice press release, as does the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I think many members of parliament participate. I know that in my riding I present trophies to boys

April 11, 1975
Youth Appreciation Week
and girls who are recognized for their achievements within the community.
Of all the letters I have read I thought the letter from our Governor General was very apropos to read into the record, especially at a time when it is to be hoped, this motion will pass. It reads as follows:
Government House Ottawa
It gives me great pleasure to join hands with the members of Optimist International to pay tribute to the Canadian youth during this Youth Appreciation Week.
In view of the growing complexities of the problems that assail us, it is encouraging to see more and more young people involving themselves in community activities, thereby sharing heavy responsibilities in many fields. Moreover, it is only by your skills and initiative that you can attain your rightful place, that of co-builders of a new society.
In the mid seventies we are faced with the uncertainties of a new era brought about by many recent changes in our social structure. Our hope for the future is that the young people of today will involve themselves in the search for the answer to our problems.
Every year in November, the Youth Appreciation Week offers us an excellent opportunity to observe and appreciate those young Canadians who have accepted the challenge of a new Canada.
I offer my warmest congratulations to all those whose merits will duly be recognized this week.
Jules Leger
I think that letter says it better than anything anyone can say in this House. I will take my seat and hope that the House will let this motion pass.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE ENCOURAGEMENT OF YOUNG PEOPLE'S ACCOMPLISHMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in just a very few words I should like to commend the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) for bringing this matter before the House at this time. I am also pleased that he has withdrawn his bill and given us a resolution instead. I say that, if for no other reason than because the resolution has a chance of being passed, and I think it is better for the House to say yes this afternoon than for it just to talk a matter out and leave it at that.
I want also to underline the view expressed by the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart) when he said that it is important that we do more than indulge in rhetoric. If we want to show appreciation of the youth of Canada we must be very specific. I will put it in as tight a nutshell as I can. I believe that if we want to show appreciation of our youth we must see to it that the Canada in which they are living and the Canada of the future will be one in which there is full employment, along with equal educational and cultural opportunities for all. It must be a place in which the housing needs of young people and their families, now and in the decades to come, are met. It must be a country in which there is full and complete health care and security down the road. It must also be a country and a world in which the air and the water are clean and where there is a secure peace. These are the kinds of things we ought to work very hard for if we really want to show appreciation of our Canadian youth.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my remarks will be brief. As a young man who, some years ago in my early teens, happened to play organized hockey

in leagues and clubs supported and sponsored by Optimist International, and also as one who, from this side of the House, was very fortunate and enjoyed participating in the game between the members of parliament and the press corps, I want on behalf of my colleagues on this side of the House who participated in that game to second the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond Delta (Mr. Reynolds) in our gratitude to the Optimist club for its sponsorship and for inviting us to participate. It was with a great deal of pleasure that each of us received from that club a very beautiful scroll and the presentation of a medallion. Certainly my gratitude is very deep.
I think it may be trite to say that the disappointing or sad things that a few of our young people get involved in sometimes receive a great deal of attention in the press, and it may also be trite to say that more good publicity on their behalf is needed and deserved. While these things might be trite to say, I do not think the truth of any of them is diminished in any way. With these few remarks I add my support for the hon. member's motion.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE ENCOURAGEMENT OF YOUNG PEOPLE'S ACCOMPLISHMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate the mover and tell him that we fully support his motion. I think Canadian youth well deserves to have its own week, and the government must take concrete action to show the interest attached to sports since youth sport is somehow the preparation of the future, the preparation of our athletes.
We are always proud to see a Canadian team able to face other competitors in true sportsmanship. I do not want to delay at all the passage of this motion, and I simply want to say that we are very proud that it was introduced before the House. We support it.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE ENCOURAGEMENT OF YOUNG PEOPLE'S ACCOMPLISHMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am extremely pleased to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) and other hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). It is good to see that he has reached his second childhood and is with us once more.
I think that I may be more appreciative of this becoming a motion rather than a bill than some hon. members. A bill is something like building for the future, and the young people today do not think that way. Some of them are saying, "I have seen the future and it will not work". That is not a bad thought because it means they are going to do something here and now about the future. They are not going to have five, ten or twenty year plans, but are setting about changing their world now and in a very successful way.
We should not forget, Madam Speaker, that boys and girls are just men and women in the cocoon. Any of us here may one day face one of them as a banker and try to borrow money from that banker, or may face one of them as a lawyer. One of the girls may be the person who comes into the room to put a large white funnel over my head, or indeed she may even be the surgeon. We have to face the fact that they are the future.
April 11, 1975

I like the idea of saying each year that we recognize the youth of the country-because each year it is a different youth. Youth passes very quickly and they should not be classified as one group. As the poet, John Oxenham, said: For every man there openeth a way A high way and a low And every man deeideth The way his soul shall go Some souls choose the high way And some souls choose the low And all the rest on misty flats Drift to and fro
But every man and woman deeideth The way their souls shall go.
I am pleased that the hon. member brought the motion forward, and pleased too that he is so anxious that all of us should agree. I am most pleased to associate myself with the motion worded in this way. I think we should remember that what we do or say is of little importance because we are really in their hands, the hands of the generation called youth; the future is theirs, not ours.
